nameStory: The bristly locust gets its name from the stiff, bristly hairs that cover its stems and branches, making it feel rough to the touch. Unlike its tall tree relatives, this is the 'bristly' member of the locust family that stays shrub-sized. The bristles are so distinctive that you can identify this plant just by running your hand along a branch!
description: Bristly locust is a medium-sized shrub that typically grows 3-8 feet tall, forming colonies through underground runners. It's covered in fragrant pink to rose-purple pea-like flowers that hang in droopy clusters during late spring and early summer. The compound leaves are made up of many small oval leaflets, giving it a delicate, feathery appearance. Despite being native to the Southeast, it's commonly planted as an ornamental in New England and sometimes escapes into the wild.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Showy pink to rose-purple flowers shaped like sweet pea blossoms, hanging in drooping clusters 2-4 inches long. The flowers are fragrant and appear in late spring to early summer.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Young stems and branches are covered with stiff, reddish-brown bristly hairs that feel rough and prickly when touched. These bristles are the plant's signature feature.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 7-13 oval leaflets arranged along a central stem. Each leaflet is smooth-edged and about 1-2 inches long, creating a feathery overall appearance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense colonies of upright stems 3-8 feet tall, spreading by underground runners. Often creates thickets in favorable locations.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flat, brown seed pods 2-3 inches long that are also covered in bristly hairs. Pods contain several small, hard seeds and persist into winter.

habitat: In New England, bristly locust is most commonly found in cultivated areas, parks, and gardens where it's been planted as an ornamental. It occasionally escapes and naturalizes along roadsides, forest edges, and disturbed soils. It prefers well-drained soils and full to partial sun, and is quite drought tolerant once established.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge in late spring, followed by the spectacular display of fragrant pink flower clusters in May and June. This is the best time for identification when the distinctive bristly stems and showy blooms are most obvious.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade and flat seed pods begin developing, still covered in the characteristic bristly hairs. Foliage remains green and lush throughout the summer months.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow before dropping, and the bristly seed pods mature to brown. The pods often persist on the plant, rattling in the wind.
seasonality.winter: Bare bristly stems are still identifiable by their rough, hairy texture and persistent seed pods. The shrub's colonial growth pattern is most visible without leaves.

funFact: Despite being called a locust, this plant is actually in the pea family and can fix nitrogen from the air into the soil through special bacteria in its roots, essentially fertilizing itself and nearby plants!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with its relatives black locust and clammy locust, but bristly locust is the only one that stays shrub-sized and has those distinctive stiff bristles covering the stems. Memory trick: 'Bristly stays bushy' - it's the short, bristly one of the locust family.
contextualKnowledge: Though called 'locust,' this plant has nothing to do with the grasshopper-like insects of the same name. The name comes from the carob tree (locust bean), which early settlers thought the seed pods resembled. As a non-native ornamental, it's generally well-behaved in New England but can spread by root suckers.
compareHints: Unlike black locust which grows into a tall tree with thorny branches, bristly locust stays shrub-sized and has soft bristles instead of hard thorns. Clammy locust is similar in size but has sticky, glandular hairs rather than dry bristles, and its flowers are usually more pink-purple. Bristly locust also has the most ornamental flowers of the three New England locusts.
